rationale: B wins because it actually sorts the same facts into cleaner reporter jobs instead of padding the board. A's "Chipotle is automating both ends of the kitchen — not just the guac" overreaches from one tested system plus one system merely "testing" and calls it a strategy before it has the receipts. B's "Flat prices, rising food costs, undisclosed labor savings: the math behind Chipotle's freeze" is the sharper founder problem: the story a finance reporter will ask whether Chipotle pitches it or not.
gaps_in_A: "Chipotle is automating both ends of the kitchen — not just the guac" turns a thin Digital Makeline testing fact into a broader automation thesis; useful thought, but underproved as a standalone angle.
"In Chipotle's test kitchens, one robot cut guacamole prep time in half" duplicates the rollout-math angle at a lower altitude; B was right to fold that proof into the 100-store story.
"call it a pilot, not a rollout" is a good skeptical frame, but it risks editorializing past the supplied fact that Autocado is rolling out to 100 restaurants.
Next step says "No clean hand-off yet" even though the set already has usable beats; the better move is pick one lane and close the named proof gap.
gaps_in_B: "100 robot-equipped stores out of more than 3,500 cannot offset chain-wide food-cost inflation" is a plausible inference, but stated too hard without the undisclosed savings, capex, food-cost exposure, or margin math.
"This beat has watched kitchen robots stall at the demo stage" adds outside industry context not in the update; likely true, but not grounded in the supplied facts.
"moving from pilot to 100 stores" is fair shorthand, but the update only says rollout to 100 and pilot kitchens halved prep time; it does not specify the exact pilot-to-rollout transition history.
The consumer price angle needs tighter handling of "food costs climb" because the update says food-cost inflation, not Chipotle's disclosed basket-level increase.
